paragraphs: The Maghāriyya take the heads of the months when the new moon appears to the eye. They have in this an argument that I shall mention when we come to treat the New Moon and its signs. It is reported of them that there were among them men who would not permit laughter. They have, on [certain] places of Scripture, far-fetched interpretations resembling idle tales.

"David son of Marwān" reported, in some of his books, of the Sadducees that they used to corporealize the Creator — exalted be His praise — taking up their statement on those descriptions which Scripture used of Him, of the descriptions that, in their plain sense, require corporealization. But of the Maghāriyya he reported the contrary of this — that they did not hold corporealization. Yet they too did not take those descriptions out of their plain sense, but claim that they are descriptions of one of the angels — the one who created the world. This is as will appear from the doctrine of "Benjamin al-Nahāwandī."
As for "Boethus" — who, we said, was the companion of "Zadok" — he used to say that the Festival of Weeks is only on the first day [of the week], as our own people [the Karaites] say.
: A notable trait ascribing extreme asceticism to the Maghāriyya; compare the descriptions of the Qumran sect in Josephus and in the scrolls themselves.

: The famous doctrine of the "created angel" of the Maghāriyya: the anthropomorphic expressions of Scripture ("the hand of the LORD," "the face of the LORD") refer to a particular world-creating angel, not to the primordial God — a doctrine resembling the Gnostic demiurge or the Philonic logos, and taken up later by Benjamin al-Nahāwandī. See Wolfson, "The Pre-Existent Angel of the Magharians and al-Nahawendi," JQR 51 (1960–61), and Erder, Mourners, chs. 2 and 6.
